reasons.C1: Testing fines, leniency and rewards on LLM sellers against a published human benchmark is policy-relevant and new; near-zero deviation finding matters for leniency design.
reasons.C2: Sound replication with scripted baselines, bootstrap and a memorization check, but one model family, four pools, and known-effect arms still pending.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 makes the human-versus-agent comparison clear, but the draft exceeds the page cap and carries 18 unresolved placeholders.

levers.C1: Show which leniency mechanism fails for agents and why, with a proposed redesign that restores reporting incentives, tested in a new arm.
levers.C2: Run the known-effect arms, a second provider and more pools, and fill every pending number with intervals before the deadline.
levers.C3: Cut to eight pages, resolve all placeholders, and lead with the low-deviation result and its implication for leniency programs.

N3.verdict: A clean, honest replication with a real policy finding; needs the pending arms and a second model to be convincing.

reasons.C1: Wash-trading detection on real agent payment rails is useful, but a funding-path rule is standard fraud analytics and wallets are not shown to be LLM agents.
reasons.C2: Labels share the rule's evidence; on independent features accuracy drops to 0.67, p = 0.14, so the headline result is likely circular.
reasons.C3: Seventeen pages against an eight-page cap; the key leakage caveat sits among many secondary numbers.

levers.C1: Tie flagged rings to verified LLM agents and show behavior a text or ledger monitor misses, making it specifically about AI collusion.
levers.C2: Obtain labels independent of transfer paths and evaluate on more held-out families, reporting a result that survives the leakage check.
levers.C3: Trim to eight pages and put the independent-feature result next to the headline accuracy in the abstract.

G7.verdict: Honest about its circularity, but that circularity undercuts the main claim, and the AI-agent link is unestablished.

reasons.C1: Non-text latent channels are a neglected oversight gap; a cheap receiver-side countermeasure is valuable, though tested only against non-adaptive senders.
reasons.C2: Strong controls: 10 of 10 reproduced checkpoints, 39 of 39 shared directions, shuffled-label probe control; no adaptive attacker or significance tests.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 carries the result in one glance, but thirteen pages exceed the cap and the link to collusion is underexplained.

levers.C1: Train channels adversarially against snapping and show whether the defense survives, turning a demonstration into a robust mitigation claim.
levers.C2: Add an adaptive channel trained through the countermeasure and a collusion task where the channel changes joint behavior.
levers.C3: Cut to eight pages and state up front why this carrier matters for colluding agents and what overseers should deploy.

F3.verdict: The most rigorous entry; the defense looks clean, but I would want an adaptive attacker before trusting it.

reasons.C1: Rival coalitions rather than coalition versus principal is a fresh framing, but coalitions are instructed and the clearing rule dominates the effect.
reasons.C2: Pre-registration with hashes, no-rival arm and 10 to 18 seeds, but no positive control, a post-freeze measure change and p = 0.055.
reasons.C3: No report seen; README and tables only, with report writing still listed as the next step.

levers.C1: Show blocs forming without instruction and rivalry changing cohesion, which would open a genuine multi-coalition research direction.
levers.C2: Add a positive control, report the pre-freeze defection measure alongside the corrected one, and power the key comparison.
levers.C3: Deliver an eight-page report with the cell figure, the Opus null result and a limitations and dual-use appendix.

M8.verdict: Interesting question and disciplined pre-registration, but the post-freeze change and missing positive control weaken trust in results.

reasons.C1: Measuring both stated acceptance and pricing behavior after a secret offer targets the say-do gap, but the design is a simple variant of known setups.
reasons.C2: No real model has been run; only mock-client tests and synthetic logs exist, so there are no results to evaluate.
reasons.C3: Design is described clearly in README and preregistration, but no report exists yet.

levers.C1: Show a measurable gap between what sellers say and what they price, across two model families, as a monitorability finding.
levers.C2: Run the 60 preregistered games on two real model families with the positive control passing and Wilson intervals reported.
levers.C3: Write the report around the say-versus-do comparison with one figure and the dual-use appendix.

H5.verdict: Careful test-first design, but with no real run forty hours out, there is nothing yet to score on execution.
